title: Supervisory Analytics Tool for SOC Assessment (SAT-SA)
description:
Background:
The National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC) assesses the cyber resilience of Critical Sector Entities (CSEs).
As part of these assessments, NCIIPC performs manual reviews of samples of security alerts and case-management records generated by Security Operations Centres (SOCs). These reviews have consistently produced valuable supervisory findings that were not evident through policies, audits, self-assessments, management reports, KPI dashboards, or compliance documentation.
The purpose of these reviews is not to assess individual alerts. Rather, alert and case-management data are used as operational evidence to assess whether a CSE possesses effective capabilities relating to:
(i). Threat Detection (ii). Investigation (iii).Escalation (iv). Incident Response (v).Security Operations (vi).Governance and Oversight (vii).Operational Discipline (viii).Cyber Resilience While effective, manual review is resource-intensive and difficult to scale across a growing number of CSEs and increasing volumes of security data.
• Description:
NCIIPC seeks a deployable Supervisory Analytics Tool for SOC Assessment (SAT-SA) that assists supervisors in analysing SOC alert and case-management data at scale.The tool should help supervisors:
(i). Identify entities requiring supervisory attention.
(ii).Prioritise alert samples and investigations for manual review.
(iii).Detect operational weaknesses and cyber resilience concerns.
(iv).Improve the efficiency, consistency and scalability of supervisory assessments.
The tool is intended to support human examiners and supervisory decision-making. It is not intended to replace supervisory judgement.
1. Out of Scope The proposed solution is not intended to:
(i). Function or replace as a Security Operations Centre (SOC) of CSEs.
(ii).Perform real-time monitoring.
(iii).Act as a SIEM platform.
(iv).Act as a centralized SOC for multiple entities.
(v).Continuously collect logs or telemetry from CSEs.
(vi).Serve as a national cyber monitoring platform.
The solution should be viewed as a supervisory analytics capability, not an operational security capability.
2. Data Environment Participants may assume access to periodic submissions including:
(i). Alert metadata (ii).Case management records (iii).Investigation workflow data (iv).Escalation records (v). Alert disposition and closure information (vi). Asset and system inventory information (where available)
Solutions should minimise dependence on raw logs, packet captures, customer information, or other sensitive operational data unless clearly justified.
3. Core Supervisory Problem Manual reviews often uncover weaknesses that are not visible through conventional reporting mechanisms.These weaknesses generally fall into two categories:
A. Execution Gaps Situations where documented controls, governance arrangements, policies, procedures, metrics or reported capabilities suggest effective operation, but operational evidence indicates otherwise.
• Examples:
(i).Alerts acknowledged but not meaningfully investigated.
(ii).Cases closed unusually quickly.
(iii).Critical alerts closed without escalation.
(iv).Repetitive or template-driven investigations.
(v).Controls deployed but not effectively monitored.
(vi).Operational behaviour designed to satisfy metrics without reducing risk.
B. Negative Space Situations where expected evidence is absent.
Examples:
(i).Missing telemetry from critical systems.
(ii).Absence of expected alert categories.
(iii).Missing investigations or escalation records.
(iv).Unexpectedly low activity levels.
(v).Monitoring blind spots.
(vi).Absence of evidence that would normally be expected within comparable environments.
The tool should help supervisors identify both known and previously unknown indicators of these conditions.
4. Functional Requirements Data Ingestion: The tool shall:
1. Ingest structured data from multiple CSEs.
2. Support common formats such as CSV, JSON, database exports and APIs where available.
3. Support analysis of large datasets spanning multiple entities and time periods.
Supervisory Analytics: The tool shall:
4. Identify indicators of detection, investigation and escalation weaknesses.
5. Detect potential execution gaps.
6. Detect potential negative space.
7. Identify anomalies, outliers and suspicious operational patterns.
8. Perform peer comparison and benchmarking across entities.
9. Generate entity-level supervisory risk indicators.
10. Prioritise entities, controls, processes and alert samples for manual review.
Explainability: The tool shall:
11. Provide clear rationale for findings.
12. Present supporting evidence.
13. Support traceability and auditability of results.
14. Allow supervisors to understand why an entity or activity was flagged.
• Reporting: The tool shall:
15. Generate supervisory dashboards and reports.
16. Support trend analysis across entities and time periods.
17. Enable drill-down from supervisory findings to underlying evidence.
• Illustrative Supervisory Use Cases The following examples are illustrative and not exhaustive.
The tool may assist in identifying:
(i). High-severity alerts closed unusually quickly.
(ii). Repeated alerts on the same asset without evidence of root-cause remediation.
(iii). Critical alerts closed without appropriate escalation.
(iv). Critical systems generating little or no security telemetry.
(v). Significant deviations from peer entities.
(vi).Missing monitoring coverage for critical environments.
(vii).Repetitive investigation patterns suggesting superficial review.
(viii).Operational behaviours that satisfy performance metrics without effectively managing cyber risk.
(ix).Investigation or escalation workloads inconsistent with expected activity levels.
Participants are encouraged to identify additional supervisory signals beyond these examples.
5.Deployment Requirements The solution shall operate within an NCIIPC-controlled environment.
The solution must:
(i).Operate in a fully offline (air-gapped) network.
(ii).Require no Internet connectivity.
(iii).Have no dependency on cloud services.
(iv).Have no dependency on SaaS platforms.
(v).Have no dependency on externally hosted AI models or APIs.
(vi).Support local deployment and local data processing.
Where AI or machine learning is proposed, participants shall specify:
(i).Model architecture.
(ii).Hardware requirements.
(iii).Offline training and inference approach.
(iv).Model update mechanism.
(v).Explainability controls.
(vi).Auditability controls.
6. Deliverables Participants should provide:
(i). Solution architecture.
(ii). Functional design.
(iii).Analytics methodology.
(iv).Data requirements.
(v).Tool or Prototype (vi).Infrastructure requirements.
(vii).Validation methodology.
(viii).Estimated deployment and operational requirements.
7. Performance Criteria Criterion Weight. Ability to Support Supervisory Assessment, Detection of Execution Gaps, Detection of Negative Space, Explainability and Auditability, Scalability and Performance, Innovation and Additional Supervisory Insights 8. Validation Requirement Participants shall explain how the proposed solution will be validated against findings derived from expert manual review.
Solutions should demonstrate their ability to identify supervisory signals, operational weaknesses and areas requiring attention with effectiveness comparable to or better than current manual sampling approaches.
9. Success Criterion A successful solution will enable NCIIPC to efficiently analyse large volumes of SOC alert and case-management data from multiple CSEs, identify entities and operational areas requiring supervisory attention, prioritise manual review effort, and preserve the quality of supervisory assurance currently obtained through expert human examination.
• Expected Solution/Deliverables for Evaluation
• Source Code Link (GitHub/Drive Link)
• Readme with Setup Instructions
• Architecture Document (Max 2 Pages)
• Demo Video (Max 2 Minutes)
• Technical Presentation (Max 5 Slides)
summary: Innovation (4/5): draws on ai, machine learning applied to a miscellaneous problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (3/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Miscellaneous. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on model, real-time, architecture. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (4/5): built to extend across states/users with modest rework. Total 22/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: Supervisory Analytics Tool for SOC Assessment (SAT-SA)

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a tool that analyzes a Security Operations Centre's alert and case-management data to automatically assess whether the SOC has effective threat detection, investigation, escalation, and governance capabilities, the kind of insight currently only found through slow, manual, resource-intensive expert review.
overview.why_it_matters: NCIIPC's manual SOC reviews consistently find real issues that policies, audits, and KPI dashboards miss entirely, but manual review doesn't scale across many organizations. Automating that analytical lens genuinely extends real oversight capability.
pain_points: Manual review of SOC alert/case data is resource-intensive and doesn't scale across many organizations.
Policies, audits, self-assessments, and KPI dashboards consistently miss issues that manual review catches.
No automated tool currently replicates the supervisory analytical judgment applied during manual review.
overview.background: NCIIPC's manual reviews of SOC alert/case-management data reveal genuine capability gaps that standard compliance documentation misses, but this manual process doesn't scale to growing numbers of Critical Sector Entities.
overview.whats_being_asked: A deployable Supervisory Analytics Tool for SOC Assessment analyzing alert and case-management data to assess SOC capabilities across threat detection, investigation, escalation, incident response, operations, governance, discipline, and resilience.
expected_solution: Automated analysis of SOC alert and case-management data.
Assessment across the eight named capability dimensions.
Findings comparable in value to manual expert review.
Deployable, scalable tool suitable for many Critical Sector Entities.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Very High. Automating genuine supervisory analytical judgment (not just compliance-checkbox auditing) that currently requires expert manual review is a real, sophisticated, largely unsolved analytical challenge.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires genuinely replicating expert analytical judgment across eight distinct capability dimensions from operational data, substantial domain and technical depth together.

competitive_landscape.note: Highly specialized, real government-oversight tooling PS, requires genuine SOC operations and cybersecurity-governance domain expertise most teams won't have.

innovation.note: Automating genuine expert supervisory judgment from operational data is a real, sophisticated, largely unsolved analytical challenge.

invention.note: Analyzing SOC operational data to infer capability quality across eight dimensions requires real analytical sophistication.

technical_feasibility.note: Real NCIIPC/SOC assessment data isn't accessible; a well-researched synthetic dataset grounded in real SOC operational patterns is the practical path.

impact_and_benefits.note: Directly extends genuine national oversight capability for critical infrastructure cyber resilience.

architecture.note: Multi-dimensional analytical assessment from alert/case data, genuine architectural and analytical sophistication.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick, one of the higher-scoring PS in this batch. Scope your demo to 2-3 of the eight named capability dimensions (e.g. Threat Detection and Escalation, which are more directly inferable from alert/case timing and routing patterns) built genuinely well, rather than shallow coverage of all eight.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Very well-specified, concrete list of eight capability dimensions gives clear, if ambitious, analytical targets.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Attempting shallow, superficial coverage of all eight dimensions would produce generic-sounding assessments that don't replicate the genuine analytical value the PS explicitly says manual review provides.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Choose 2-3 capability dimensions that are most directly inferable from alert/case-management data patterns (e.g. escalation timing patterns, investigation-to-resolution timelines) and build genuinely insightful analysis for those, rather than shallow coverage of all eight.

idea_0_4: Research real SOC operational patterns and what alert/case-management data typically reveals about capability quality.
Choose 2-3 capability dimensions to analyze deeply (e.g. Threat Detection and Escalation).
Split: one person on synthetic SOC dataset construction, one on the analytical assessment logic.
prototype_4_22: Construct a realistic synthetic SOC alert/case-management dataset with embedded capability-quality signals (both strong and weak examples).
Build your analytical logic for your chosen capability dimensions.
Test that your analysis correctly distinguishes your embedded strong versus weak capability examples.
integration_22_30: Refine your analytical logic based on discrimination test results.
Build the assessment report output with clear, explainable findings.
Test against a genuinely ambiguous case to see how your tool handles uncertainty.
polish_30_36: Build a clear supervisory-assessment report output.
Rehearse presenting your analysis on your synthetic data, explaining what specific data patterns drove your findings.
Prepare to discuss your scoping choice (2-3 dimensions) and what full eight-dimension coverage would require.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show your tool correctly distinguishing a genuinely strong-capability synthetic SOC example from a weak one, with specific, explainable reasoning tied to actual data patterns (e.g. escalation timing, investigation completeness), that discrimination, grounded in real SOC operational understanding, is the actual hard, valuable analytical capability this PS is asking to replicate.

strengths: Very well-specified, concrete capability dimensions give clear analytical targets.
Genuine, high-level national-security relevance if built with real domain grounding.
weaknesses: Real NCIIPC/SOC assessment data isn't accessible, synthetic realism is the key credibility factor.
Full eight-dimension coverage at genuine analytical depth isn't achievable in 36 hours, requires deliberate scoping.

team_fit.ideal_ratio: Don't skip SOC domain research, this PS's entire value depends on genuinely understanding what good versus poor SOC operational patterns actually look like.
team_fit.approach: Research real SOC operational maturity models and what alert/case-management data patterns indicate about capability quality before building analytical logic.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard data analysis and reporting scaffolding.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Understanding what alert/case-management data patterns genuinely indicate about SOC capability quality across each dimension, that requires real cybersecurity operations and governance domain expertise, the exact expertise this PS explicitly says is currently only found in manual expert review.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: An AI-scaffolded assessment tool without genuine SOC operations domain grounding would likely produce generic, unhelpful findings that don't replicate the actual analytical insight manual expert review provides, missing the entire point of this PS.

data_resource_availability.status: Real NCIIPC/CSE SOC assessment data isn't accessible to a hackathon team; a well-researched synthetic dataset grounded in real SOC operational maturity concepts is the practical and appropriate path.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: Construct a synthetic SOC alert/case-management dataset grounded in published SOC maturity-model research, clearly labeled as synthetic but domain-grounded.

judge_qna.question: How does your tool actually infer SOC capability quality from raw alert/case data, not just count metrics?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Walk through your specific analytical approach for one capability dimension, e.g. how escalation timing patterns and case-routing behavior reveal genuine escalation-capability quality, not just alert volume.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's the difference between your analysis and a simple KPI dashboard, which the problem statement says already exists and misses these issues?

judge_qna.question: Why did you choose these 2-3 capability dimensions instead of covering all eight?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Explain your prioritization, these dimensions are most directly inferable from alert/case-management data patterns specifically, and describe what additional data sources the other dimensions would need.
judge_qna.follow_up: What data would you need to genuinely assess Governance and Oversight, which seems less directly inferable from alert data alone?
